newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union spurns Chrysler 60 hrs before deadline.
newsitem.headline: Canada union spurns Chrysler 60 hrs before deadline.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union Sunday rejected a sweetened economic offer from Chrysler Corp. saying that they had "miles to go" on key issues with less than 60 hours left before a Tuesday midnight strike deadline.
Wearing T-shirts that said "Outsource this, Eh!" union members met with Chrysler for nearly an hour before rejecting a second financial proposal from Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit.

"Ken Lewenza (Chrysler bargaining committee chairman) and myself express the disappointment of the bargaining committee with about 60 hours left to conclude an agreement here that we were so far short in so many different areas," said Buzz Hargrove, president of the CAW.

Hargrove said the economic package fell far short of the union's expectations on wage increases, early retirement programs and still included demands of concessions and user co-pay fees from the union's health and benefit plans.
However Chrysler Canada's lead negotiator, Ken Francese, said he thought the proposal was a step forward and suggested the parties still had time and room to get a deal.
"They weren't ready to sign on the dotted line and we have some more work to do, but we have some time to do it," Francese said.
The Chrysler negotiator said both sides will meet later on Sunday afternoon over the key issue of outsourcing to talk over the company's latest offer.
"We're going to have more discussion on that today and hopefully we'll be a lot closer at the end of today to resolving that issue," Francese said.
Outsourcing is the sale of plants or the transfer of work to outside contractors, whose employees are generally not members of the auto unions.

The CAW's Hargrove said this latest outsourcing offer could be the key deal maker to open up talks and head both sides towards an agreement before the strike deadline, if it allays the union's concerns over job security.
"If this outsourcing proposal has some good things in it, it may break the logjam," Hargrove said.
Hargrove likened outsourcing to allowing companies the right to sell crack-cocaine and said it should be stopped because it was wrecking families, communities and the nation.

"The reasons we outlaw it (the sale of crack) and don't allow it to happen is because it wrecks families, wrecks communities, it wrecks nations, so why wouldn't we outlaw the ability of the corporations who are making a lot of money to wreck families, wreck communities and wreck our nation with this (outsourcing) idea," he said.

The CAW is the largest private-sector union in Canada with more than 200,000 members in various sectors of the economy. About 53,000 members work for the auto companies and 12,600 of them work for Chrysler alone.

The union has said that outsourcing is its biggest issue and it has been rocked by announcements this year that General Motors Corp.'s Canadian subsidiary intends to sell two parts plants in Canada and shed more than 5,000 jobs.

Chrysler is the CAW's first of three negotiating targets and the union will try to craft an agreement on outsourcing, wages and benefits to use as a pattern for deals with Ford Motor Co.'s Canadian unit and General Motors of Canada.
